title: The discovery of radioactivity
subtitle: Marie Curie
subject: sciences
description: Marie Curie, with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, opens the chapter of radioactivity. Two Nobel Prizes, overwhelming work, and an immense legacy.

hero.hook: She weighed tons of ore to isolate a few grams of an invisible element.

blocks.text: **Marie Curie** (born Maria Skłodowska) is the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize. She remains the only person to have received **two** in two different sciences: physics, then chemistry.
Its subject: **radioactivity**, that is to say the fact that certain atoms spontaneously send energy and particles.
Born in Poland, she went to study in Paris because local universities closed many doors to women. She works hard, often in precarious conditions.
She married **Pierre Curie**, physicist. Together, they formed a rare laboratory duo for the time.
In **1896**, **Henri Becquerel** noticed that uranium veils photographic plates without light. Marie Curie decides to study this phenomenon in detail. She invented the word **radioactivity**.

blocks.caption: Tons of pitchblende to isolate radium and polonium.

blocks.text: With Pierre, she discovers two new elements: **polonium** (named after Poland) and **radium**. To isolate them, enormous quantities of ore, pitchblende, must be processed.
Radium glows faintly in the dark. We were amazed at first… before understanding how dangerous it was.
In **1903**, Marie, Pierre and Becquerel received the Nobel Prize in physics. In **1911**, Marie alone received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Pierre died accidentally in 1906. She continues.
During the First World War, she organized mobile x-ray units to treat the wounded. She exposes her body to doses that today we would know are unacceptable.
Radioactivity has enabled radiotherapy against certain cancers… and also nuclear weapons. Knowledge is neutral; its uses are not.
Marie Curie transformed a strange observation into a new science: radioactivity. His work opened up modern physics… at the cost of risks then poorly understood.
